q: Which type of learning is explicitly NOT part of the data mining module?
why: Reinforcement learning is listed as one of the 4 ML categories but marked '(this will not be part of the DM module)'.

q: In CRISP-DM, the conclusions or inferences drawn from the models and from the data mining process are called:
why: Evaluation phase: '...These are known as findings.'

q: In the lecture's 'Types of Learning' list, Logistic Regression appears under:
why: Classification examples: Decision Tree, Neural Networks, Logistic Regression. Don't let the word 'Regression' fool you.

q: Which statement matches the lecture's position on ethics?
options: Proxy attributes such as area code are ethically neutral
Removing names is enough to anonymize data
Using race as an attribute is unethical in every application
Purely statistical arguments are never sufficient
why: The ethical situation depends on the application (the same information may be fine in a medical setting), and area code can correlate with race. 'Purely statistical arguments are never sufficient!'

q: About what proportion of the effort is spent on data cleaning / data preparation?
why: Both the KDD and CRISP-DM slides say about 60%.

q: In CRISP-DM, splitting the data into training and test sets belongs to which phase?
why: The slide lists splitting into training and test sets under Data Preparation, together with merging, sampling, aggregating, deriving attributes, sorting and handling blanks.

q: ML models are evaluated in the Evaluation phase of CRISP-DM against:
options: The business success criteria established at the start of the project
The accuracy on the training set
why: 'Evaluate the results of your efforts using the business success criteria established at the beginning of the project.'

q: Why does association learning need constraints such as minimum coverage and minimum accuracy?
options: Because rules can predict any attribute (and several at once), so there are far more association rules than classification rules
Because association can only handle numeric attributes
Because without class labels accuracy cannot be computed
why: Association rules can predict any attribute's value, and more than one at a time. That gives far more rules, so constraints are necessary.

q: According to the ethics slide, about 85% of Americans can be identified from:
options: Name, zip code and phone number
Zip code, birth date and sex
why: This shows why anonymizing data is difficult: zip code + birth date + sex identifies about 85%.

q: Success in clustering is often measured:
options: Objectively, on test data with known labels
Using minimum coverage and minimum accuracy
why: Clustering is unsupervised, so 'success is often measured subjectively'. Classification success is measured objectively.

q: Data mining is best described as:
options: The analysis step of the KDD process
The entire Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) process
why: The slides: 'DM is the analysis step of the knowledge discovery in databases process, or KDD.' It is not the whole of KDD.

q: According to the lecture, the underlying reason for inaccurate values is:
options: Data has not been collected for mining
why: Inaccurate values: 'Reason: Data has not been collected for mining.'

q: Which statistics can be computed for a NOMINAL attribute?
why: Nominal values only support equality tests, so you can find the count and the mode.

q: A medical test value is missing for some patients. What does the lecture warn?
options: The missingness may be significant in itself, so 'missing' may need to be coded as an extra value
Missing values can always be safely replaced by the mean
Instances with missing values must always be deleted
Missing values only arise from typos
why: Example: a missing test in a medical examination. Most schemes assume missingness is not significant, but it may be. And always report the action you took.

q: The main limitation of univariate (boxplot) outlier detection is that it:
options: Cannot detect unusual combinations of multiple variables
why: In the 2-feature example, the boxplot shows no outliers but the scatter plot does. Multivariate methods are needed.

q: Which is NOT one of the five EDA steps in the lecture?
why: The 5 steps are Data Cleaning, Statistical Analysis, Data Visualization, Detect Outliers and Data Transformation.

q: A dense cluster of points sits right at the boundary of a boxplot whisker. According to the lecture they should:
why: Outliers are points significantly removed from the main body. A cluster right at the whisker boundary should typically not be removed.

q: By default, the whiskers of a Seaborn boxplot extend to:
why: Whiskers are by default ±1.5 IQR. Points beyond them are possible outliers and candidates for removal.

q: According to the lecture, which statement about scaling is TRUE?
options: Standardization is less sensitive to outliers than normalization
Normalization transforms features to mean 0 and SD 1
why: Normalization means [0,1] (MinMaxScaler) and standardization means mean 0, SD 1. The slide says standardization is less sensitive to outliers. fit_transform returns a NumPy array.

q: Treating degrees on a compass in a special way is an example of which kind of metadata?
why: Metadata examples: dimensional considerations, circular orderings (compass degrees), partial orderings (generalization/specialization).

q: Temperature as 'hot > mild > cool' is ordinal. Which statement is TRUE?
options: The distance between hot and mild equals that between mild and cool
Order is defined but distance between values is not
It has a true zero point
why: Ordinal imposes an order but no distance between values; addition and subtraction don't make sense.

q: Which technique does the lecture name as one of the most popular for MULTIVARIATE outlier detection?
why: DBSCAN treats low-density regions as noise/outliers. Note that it expects standardized data.

q: Which scikit-learn class performs range normalisation to [0, 1]?
why: preprocessing.MinMaxScaler().

q: Temperature measured in degrees Fahrenheit is an example of which level of measurement?
why: It is ordered with fixed equal units, but the zero point is not defined, so it is interval. Year is also interval.

q: According to the 'Data Types Suitability' slide, which algorithms are suited to NOMINAL data?
options: Logistic regression, decision trees and association (Apriori, FP-Growth)
why: Nominal: logistic regression, decision trees, association. Ratio (easy distance metrics): neural networks, linear regression, clustering.

q: For the attribute 'year', which statement is valid?
options: The difference between 2020 and 2010 is meaningful
Adding two years gives a meaningful value
why: Interval data: differences make sense; sums, products and ratios don't. All operations are allowed only for ratio data.

q: Multi-instance learning: which application is given as an example?
why: In multi-instance learning each example is a set of instances, and one or more of them may be responsible for the classification. The example given is drug activity prediction.

q: A KNN dataset has many features in [0,1] and one feature in [−1000, 1000]. Without scaling:
options: All features contribute equally to the distance
The KNN would essentially rely on the single large-range feature
why: The small-range features become uninformative in the Euclidean distance, which is why scaling is needed.

q: In PCA, the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are:
options: The coefficients attached to the components
The directions of the axes with the most variance
why: Eigenvectors are the directions of most variance; eigenvalues are the coefficients attached to them. Components are ranked by variance.

q: How should an ORDINAL feature such as Grade (A, B, C...) be encoded according to the lecture?
options: Manually with a mapping dictionary and the DataFrame map method
Automatically with OrdinalEncoder, which knows the order
why: Ordering is domain-specific, so there is no automatic mechanism. Specify the mapping manually, e.g. {'F':0,...,'A':4} with df['Grade'].map(...).

q: The main disadvantage of one-hot encoding, and the suggested mitigation, are:
options: Loss of order; fix with a mapping dictionary
It cannot handle strings; use OrdinalEncoder
It is sensitive to outliers; use standardization
Many distinct values create many features (long training, poorer models); mitigate with PCA
why: The rapid increase in dimensionality can be reduced with dimensionality reduction such as PCA.

q: What does pandas get_dummies do?
options: Converts string columns and leaves the other columns unadjusted
why: Straight from the slide.

q: Three boxes: A = 4 red; B = 3 red + 1 blue; C = 2 red + 2 blue. Which has the HIGHEST entropy?
why: A = 0, B ≈ 0.811, C = 1 bit, the maximum for 2 classes (equally likely).

q: Which statement about FILTER feature selection methods is TRUE?
options: They rank attributes without building a model, and are less likely to detect dependencies/redundancies
They create new features as linear combinations
They build a model to evaluate each subset
They are slow but give the best results
why: Filters are quicker and more scalable, normally univariate. Building models describes wrappers; linear combinations describe PCA.

q: The entropy of a box with 3 red and 1 blue ball (log base 2) is approximately:
Which feature selection approach is 'very heavy in terms of computation but gets the best results'?
why: Wrappers build models to evaluate subsets of features: very costly, but the best results, and useful for interpretability.

q: PCA's main drawback, according to the lecture:
options: It increases the number of features
The new features are combinations of variables, so they are not possible to understand
why: PCA is quick and reduces the space, but the components aren't interpretable.

q: What is the FIRST step of PCA?
why: First standardize, then calculate the covariance between all variables.

q: The lecture distinguishes 'explainability' and 'interpretability'. Feature selection is said to improve:
why: Benefits: understanding the data, improving interpretability (note: explainability ≠ interpretability), accuracy, and speed.

q: Using OrdinalEncoder on the nominal feature Department (Biology, Chemistry, Computing) causes what problem?
options: The algorithm assumes an order: Computing > Chemistry > Biology
It raises an error on strings
why: The integers imply an ordering that doesn't exist. The fix is one-hot encoding.

q: Using the lecture's feature-selection decision tree: you need to UNDERSTAND the result and the data does NOT have a lot of features. Which method?
why: Understand: yes, then lots of features → Filter, otherwise → Wrapper. Understand: no, then small model or small dataset → PCA, otherwise → Deep Learning.

q: Play-golf data: H = 0.940 and E(PlayGolf, Outlook) = 0.693. The information gain of Outlook is:
why: IG = entropy before − entropy after = 0.940 − 0.693 = 0.247, the highest, so Outlook is the root.

q: Gene study: 70 patients, 20,000 fields each, and you need to know WHICH genes matter. Following the decision tree:
why: You need to understand the result and there are many features, so Filter. A wrapper would be far too expensive with 20k features.

q: min_samples_leaf is:
options: The minimum number of samples a node must have before it can be split
The number of features considered per split
The minimum number of samples a leaf node must have
why: 'Minimum samples a node must have before it can be split' describes min_samples_split.

q: Which statement about Gini vs Entropy is TRUE?
options: Gini tends to isolate the most frequent class in its own branch; entropy gives slightly more balanced trees
Entropy is faster to compute, so it is the default
They usually produce very different trees
C4.5 uses Gini and CART uses entropy
why: Gini is slightly faster (a good default) and used by CART; entropy is used by C4.5/J48. They usually lead to similar trees.

q: Why are decision trees sensitive to rotation of the training data?
options: Their decision boundaries are perpendicular to the axes
why: A linearly separable set rotated 45° gives a convoluted staircase boundary that generalizes poorly.

q: In a decision tree, which statement is TRUE?
options: Numeric attributes always get a three-way split
A numeric attribute may be tested several times on the same path
A nominal attribute may be tested many times on the same path
why: A nominal attribute won't be tested more than once; a numeric one may be. Leaves need not be pure (identical instances can have different classes).

q: Why is error on the training data NOT a useful estimator for pruning?
options: It would result in almost no pruning
It is too expensive to compute
why: The alternatives are a hold-out set (reduced-error pruning) or C4.5's confidence-based estimate.

q: x1 = 1..8 with y = 0,0,0,1,1,1,1,1 (parent Gini = 15/32). Which split gives the larger Gini decrease?
why: Splitting at 3.5 makes both children pure, so the whole 15/32 is removed.

q: Which statement about the CART algorithm is FALSE?
options: It splits on a single feature k and a threshold tk
It is guaranteed to find the optimal tree
It minimizes the size-weighted impurity of the two subsets
why: CART is greedy: it does not look ahead several levels, so it produces a reasonably good solution that is not guaranteed optimal.

q: Comparing the postpruning operations:
options: Subtree raising is faster than subtree replacement
Subtree raising is slower than subtree replacement
why: Subtree replacement works bottom-up. Subtree raising deletes a node and redistributes instances, which makes it slower.

q: The prediction complexity of a (roughly balanced) decision tree is about:
options: O(n × m log m), depending on the number of features
O(log2 m), independent of the number of features
why: Prediction traverses root to leaf, checking one feature per node. O(n × m log m) is the TRAINING complexity.

q: A node contains 0 Setosa, 49 Versicolor and 5 Virginica. Its Gini impurity is about:
An 'ID code' attribute gets the maximal information gain (0.940 bits). This illustrates that:
options: Information gain is biased toward attributes with many values, which can cause overfitting
ID codes are the best predictors
Entropy cannot be computed for nominal data
why: Every single-instance subset is pure (entropy 0), so the gain is maximal, but the split is useless for prediction. It also causes data fragmentation.

q: Which impurity function is the ONLY one that satisfies all three wishlist properties (zero when pure, max when uniform, multistage)?
why: 'It can be shown that entropy is the only function that satisfies all three properties.' The multistage property is not strictly necessary in practice.

q: A regression decision tree predicts, for each region:
options: A linear function of the features
The average target value of the training instances in that region
why: CART for regression minimizes MSE (not Gini or entropy), and each leaf predicts the mean target.

q: For a 2-class problem, the MAXIMUM possible Gini impurity is:
why: The maximum is 1 − 1/k = 0.5 for k = 2. Trap: the slide says 'a Gini coefficient of 1 expresses maximal inequality', but impurity never reaches 1.

q: A flower reaches a leaf containing 0 Setosa, 49 Versicolor and 5 Virginica. The predicted probability of Versicolor is:
why: The tree returns the ratio of training instances of class k in that leaf: 49/54 = 90.7%.

q: The XOR/parity problem illustrates which danger?
options: Prepruning may stop growth too early (early stopping)
why: No single attribute is significantly associated with the class, so prepruning won't even expand the root. XOR-type problems are rare in practice, though.

q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a disadvantage of decision trees?
options: Must regrow the tree when adding training instances
why: 'Can handle missing data' is listed as a PRO.

q: In C4.5's pruning method, the default confidence c = 25% corresponds to z =
why: If c = 25% then z = 0.69 (from the normal distribution).

q: Which pruning strategy is preferred in practice?
why: Postpruning is preferred because prepruning can 'stop early'. Prepruning is faster, which is why the 'prepruning, because it is faster' option is a trap.

q: Decision trees are called NON-parametric because:
options: They only work on nominal data
The number of parameters is not determined prior to training
why: The structure is free to stick closely to the data (risk of overfitting). Parametric models such as linear models have a fixed number of parameters (risk of underfitting).

q: Quinlan's classic tree learner ID3 used which test in addition to information gain for prepruning?
why: Only statistically significant attributes (chi-squared) could be selected by the information gain procedure.

q: The 'zero-frequency problem' in Naïve Bayes is fixed by:
options: Adding 1 to every attribute value–class count (Laplace estimator)
why: Probabilities are then never zero. A further advantage: it stabilizes estimates computed from small samples.

q: Basis functions φ help SVMs with non-linearly separable data because:
options: They make the data normally distributed
There are typically more basis functions than features, which moves the data into a higher-dimensional space where a linear separator is expected to exist
why: Example: z = x² + y² turns a circular boundary into a flat plane.

q: The support vectors are:
options: The extreme points closest to the hyperplane that define the margin
The points farthest from the hyperplane
why: 'SVM chooses the extreme points/vectors that help in creating the hyperplane.'

q: How does Naïve Bayes handle a missing attribute value at CLASSIFICATION time?
options: Replaces it with the class mean
Omits the attribute from the calculation
Treats it as a separate value
why: During training the instance isn't counted for that combination; during classification the attribute is omitted.

q: Training an SVM is framed as:
why: It is defined by a set of constraints, ti(w0 + w·d) ≥ 1, and an optimization criterion (maximize 2/||w||).

q: In Naïve Bayes with Gaussian attributes, a computed density f(x) = 1.4. This is:
options: A sign of an error in σ
Possible, since densities can exceed 1 (they must integrate to 1)
why: Densities are not probabilities, but when computing likelihoods you can treat them like probabilities.

q: How does 1R handle missing values?
options: It treats 'missing' as a separate attribute value
It replaces them with the mode
It omits the attribute from the calculation
why: Contrast with Naïve Bayes, which omits the attribute during classification.

q: When estimating mean and SD for a numeric attribute in Naïve Bayes, missing values are:
why: 'Missing values during training are not included in calculation of mean and standard deviation.'

q: Which situation causes problems for Naïve Bayes according to the lecture?
options: Having small datasets with Laplace smoothing
why: Identical attributes effectively count the same evidence several times. For non-normal numeric attributes, kernel density estimators can be used.

q: In Bayes' rule P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E), the PRIOR probability of H is:
why: Prior = P(H) (before evidence); posterior = P(H|E) (after evidence). Watch out: the slide has the two formulas swapped.

q: The α parameters in the SVM model are:
options: Lagrange multipliers, one per support vector
why: M(q) = Σ (ti × α[i] × (di·q) + w0), summed over the s support vectors.

q: Why does Naïve Bayes work well even when the independence assumption is clearly violated?
options: Because attributes are always independent in practice
Classification only needs the maximum probability assigned to the correct class, not accurate probabilities
why: However, adding too many redundant (e.g. identical) attributes will cause problems.

q: In SVM, the size of the margin is:
why: The distance from the margin extent to the boundary is 1/||w||, and the margin is symmetric, so 2/||w||. Training maximizes it.

q: Why does a timestamp attribute look perfect for 1R?
options: It gets zero errors because every value is unique, which is overfitting
why: Discretization is very sensitive to noise and unique values. The fix is a minimum number of majority-class instances per interval.

q: In the generalized Laplace estimate (2 + μp1)/(9 + μ), the weights p1, p2, p3:
options: Need not be equal but must sum to 1
why: 'Weights don't need to be equal (but they must sum to 1).'

q: New day: Sunny, Cool, High, Windy=True. Likelihoods: yes = 0.0053, no = 0.0206. P(no) is about:
What is the main purpose of the kernel trick?
options: To avoid the expensive dot product of basis-function-transformed vectors by computing it from the original features
To reduce the number of support vectors
why: k(x,z) = ⟨φ(x), φ(z)⟩. We can use a kernel without knowing φ, as long as we can prove such a mapping exists.

q: The two assumptions of Naïve Bayes are that attributes are:
options: Equally important and statistically independent given the class
Independent of the class and of each other
why: The independence assumption is almost never correct, but the scheme often works surprisingly well.

q: The Gaussian radial basis kernel is:
why: γ is a manually chosen tuning parameter. d·q + c is the linear kernel, (d·q + 1)^p the polynomial kernel, and tanh is not covered.

q: In Holte's (1993) 1R study, the minimum number of instances in the majority class per interval was set to:
why: Holte set it to 6 after experimentation. The lecture's own worked example used 3, which is the trap.

q: On the weather data, which attributes have the lowest 1R total error (4/14)?
why: Outlook 4/14, Temperature 5/14, Humidity 4/14, Windy 5/14. It's a tie.

q: Which clustering approach is 'based on a multiple-level granularity structure'?
why: Model-based hypothesizes a model for each cluster and finds the best fit.

q: Minkowski distance with q = 1 is:
why: q = 1 gives Manhattan, q = 2 gives Euclidean.

q: p is a core point and q (a border point) lies in p's ε-neighbourhood. Which is TRUE?
options: p is directly density-reachable from q
Neither is reachable from the other
q is directly density-reachable from p, but not vice versa
why: Direct density-reachability requires the SOURCE to be a core point, so it is not symmetric.

q: Points (3,4), (2,6), (4,5), (4,7), (3,8). The clustering feature CF = (N, LS, SS) is:
why: LS is the linear sum (16, 30); SS is the square sum (9+4+16+16+9, 16+36+25+49+64) = (54, 190).

q: Hierarchical clustering:
options: Does not require k, but needs a termination condition
why: It uses the distance matrix. It can never undo what was done previously, and it is at least O(n²).

q: In the Jack/Mary/Jim example, why is gender excluded?
why: Gender is symmetric; the remaining (asymmetric) attributes are used with Jaccard.

q: Which is a major feature of density-based clustering?
options: It discovers clusters of arbitrary shape and handles noise
It needs many scans of the data
why: Also: one scan, and it needs density parameters as the termination condition.

q: Which statement about PAM (k-medoids) is TRUE?
options: It works effectively for small data sets but does not scale well
Each cluster is represented by its mean
why: Medoids are real objects in the cluster.

q: A good clustering produces:
options: High inter-class similarity and low intra-class similarity
High intra-class similarity and low inter-class similarity
High similarity both within and between clusters
why: Intra means within a cluster (should be similar); inter means between clusters (should be dissimilar).

q: How does the lecture suggest choosing Eps for DBSCAN?
options: Plot the sorted distances of every point to its k-th nearest neighbour
Use the elbow of the SSE curve
why: Noise points have their k-th nearest neighbour farther away. Pick Eps where the curve rises sharply.

q: For ASYMMETRIC binary variables, which dissimilarity is appropriate?
why: Jaccard ignores d (negative matches, 0/0). Simple matching is for symmetric variables.

q: An ordinal variable has M = 5 levels. A value with rank r = 3 is mapped to:
why: z = (r − 1)/(M − 1) = 2/4 = 0.5. It is then treated as interval-scaled.

q: k-means often terminates at a local optimum. According to the lecture, the global optimum may be found using:
why: Exhaustively enumerating all partitions also finds it, but that is infeasible.

q: CURE improves hierarchical clustering by:
options: Selecting well-scattered points from a cluster and shrinking them towards the centre by a fraction
why: BIRCH is the one that uses a CF-tree.

q: When standardizing interval-scaled variables for clustering, the lecture uses the mean absolute deviation because it is:
options: More robust to outliers than the standard deviation
why: Deviations aren't squared, so outliers have less effect. Then z = (x − m)/s.

q: In DBSCAN, a BORDER point is one that:
options: Is neither core nor in any core's neighbourhood
Has fewer than MinPts within Eps but lies in the neighbourhood of a core point
Has at least MinPts neighbours within Eps
why: 'Neither core nor in any core's neighbourhood' describes a noise point. Core, border and noise are mutually exclusive.

q: Jim vs Mary (asymmetric binary): a = 1, b = 1, c = 2. The Jaccard dissimilarity is:
To cluster purely CATEGORICAL data with a k-means-style approach, use:
why: k-modes uses modes instead of means. k-prototype handles mixed categorical + numeric data.

q: The time complexity of k-means is:
why: t iterations, k clusters, n objects, with k and t much smaller than n. It is relatively efficient.

q: Which is NOT a weakness of k-means?
options: The number of clusters k must be specified in advance
It cannot handle noisy data and outliers well
It is computationally infeasible for large n
It is not suitable for non-convex cluster shapes
why: k-means is relatively efficient, O(tkn). (It is applicable only when a mean is defined.)

q: For a nominal variable, simple matching dissimilarity is d = (p − m)/p, where:
options: m = number of matches, p = total number of variables
p = number of matches, m = total variables
why: Alternative: create one binary variable per nominal state.

q: In PAM, a medoid i is replaced by non-medoid h when the total swapping cost TCih is:
why: A negative cost means the total distance improves.

q: DBSCAN does NOT work well when:
why: It is also sensitive to its parameters (Eps 9.92 vs 9.75 gave very different results).

q: AGNES and DIANA are respectively:
why: AGNES uses single-link, merging the least dissimilar nodes until everything is one cluster. DIANA is the inverse.
